course_description:
This course builds on your developing knowledge and skills in social work by focusing on practice with groups and communities. We will explore two key methods of social work: group work practice and community work practice, often referred to as mezzo and macro practice. Both these methods focus on social work practice in building and sustaining groups and communities.

Welcome to SWSP2088: Direct Practice 2

In conjunction with SWSP2077 Direct Practice 1, which focused on direct practice with individuals in both voluntary and involuntary casework settings, SWSP2088 aims to facilitate the development of your practice skills and theoretical understandings to enable you to undertake a field placement involving group and community work practice. As with SWSP2077, this course begins by exploring social work practice as a purposeful activity. We consider how we negotiate practice purpose through our context, our professional base, as well as the values, experiences, skills and perspectives that we bring to social work. This course builds on your existing skills base and introduces competencies for effective social work practice with groups and communities.

Core Knowledge and Concepts

In SWSP2088, you will build foundational knowledge and skills for working with groups and communities, grounded in social work values and informed by a critically reflective approach. We will examine diverse forms of community, including spatial communities (such as urban and rural communities) and identity-based communities. The course explores key theories of community work practice, comparing consensual and contestual approaches. A central focus is placed on two models of community development practice: Asset Based Community Development (ABCD) and Anti-Oppressive Practice (AOP). You will also develop knowledge of community engagement and advocacy , including processes of community consultation and strategies for working at the interface of policy and practice. This includes learning about how community workers advocate with and for communities, and support access to resources.

Direct Practice Skills

In SWSP2088, you acquire a range of introductory direct practice skills for working with groups and communities. These include designing and facilitating community education processes, planning and running community support groups and demonstrating inclusive group leadership that maximises group participation and ensures that all voices are heard in groups and meetings. You will develop skills in assessing community strengths and capacities, managing conflict in group or community settings, and conducting community consultations and advocacy processes. The course also introduces practical skills in preparing media releases for print and online platforms, writing funding submissions for small-scale community projects and evaluating the impact and effectiveness of community-based practice.

Acknowledgement

The University of Queensland acknowledges the Traditional Owners and their custodianship of the lands on which the university now stands. We pay our respects to their Ancestors and their descendants, who continue their cultural and spiritual connections to Country. We recognise their valuable contributions to Australia and global society.ﾠ

ASWEAS Required Curriculum Content Areas covered in this course:

The Bachelor of Social Work (Hons) program is accredited by the Australian Association of Social Workers. The Australian Social Work Education and Accreditation Standards (2020) stipulates that accredited social work programs are required to include content that addresses the five core curriculum areas listed below. This course contains content in the following curriculum areas:

1. Constructions of social work purpose, place, and practice

2. Power, oppression, and exploitation

4. Culture, identity, and discrimination

5. Psychosocial health and wellbeing across the lifecycle

The BSocWk(Hons) program is undergoing re-accreditation in 2026.

learning_outcomes.description: Articulate relevant theoretical frameworks for group and community work, and recognise different forms of community, and the implications for inclusive social work practice.
Demonstrate how social work values inform group and community practice and contribute to culturally responsive and inclusive approaches with diverse communities.
Apply research skills to access and interpret data on community needs and capacities and use this evidence to inform effective community consultation and practice decisions.
Apply foundational social work skills in engaging, assessing and intervening with groups and communities, including the use of community education processes.
Use community consultation skills and community work methods to contribute to influencing and implementing social policy.

assessment_details.task_description: This description is a brief summary of the assessment task. For full details, including the marking rubric, please refer to the course Learn UQ (Blackboard Ultra) site. The assessment consists of two parts. Part A: Group Workshop [Group Task - Secure] Weighting: 30% Description: In the four tutorials from Week 4 (21 August) to Week 7 (11 September), students will work in groups (4 students in each group) to develop and then lead/facilitate one of four community work practice skills workshops. Students who are not leading the weekly workshops will attend as participants and reflect on the workshop. The skills workshops are an opportunity for students to develop and apply group work and community work practice skills. Group Allocations: Your tutor will organise group membership, topics and the workshop schedule in your first tutorial of the semester (Week 2). Please ensure that you attend this class. If you are unable to attend, you will be placed in a group and provided the contact details of your group members. It is your responsibility to make contact with your group as soon as possible upon receipt of these details. Tutorial Participation Requirement: Your participation in the skills workshops in Week 4, Week 5, Week 6 and Week 7 is necessary to meet the learning outcomes required by Australian Association of Social Workers (AASW) accreditation standards. Therefore, your tutor will be taking attendance in these weeks. If a member of the team is ill, then remainder of the team will facilitate their workshop and indicate which section the absent student was to facilitate. The student who was absent will then facilitate that section of the workshop in their tutorial group in a subsequent tutorial timeslot. Part B: Individual Reflective Journaling Activity (completed and submitted each week) [Individual - Secure] Weighting: 20% Description: For this assessment, each student will write 4 journal entries in class time, one for each of the four workshops in Week 4, Week 5, Week 6 and Week 7. In each entry, students will write their response to a reflective prompt provided in each workshop to be completed in class time. Each entry will be written on a separate Task Sheet and submitted to your course tutor at the end of the writing period. If a student is unable to attend and participate in the community work skills tutorials due to illness or an unexpected personal crisis, they will have the opportunity to submit a catch-up reflective journal entry (Part B) on the same topic as the workshop missed. This will be scheduled by your tutor in consultation with the course coordinator. Students will be required to present a medical certificate or evidence of an unanticipated personal crisis that prevented their participation in the tutorial on that day to remain eligible to submit a journal entry for a missed workshop. Please note that if you do not have the required supporting evidence, you will not be offered an opportunity to make up the reflection task and are thus not eligible for the 5 marks for that week’s reflection. assessment_details.submission_guidelines:
Part A: Group Workshop [Submission]
Each group needs to provide the following details about their workshop and upload to Turnitin by 12pm on the day before your workshop:
Names of Students in the Group Date of Presentation Summary of preparation process (please list each group member and identify the tasks they completed in preparation for the workshop) Outline of the workshop activities A few bullet points (full sentences) indicating what feedback on your workshop would be most useful to your group. Acknowledgment of source materials/resources/references. Please include acknowledgement of AI resources if used to assist with preparing your workshop. However, please note that this assessment is designated as a secure assessment, designed to protect academic integrity and your understanding of course concepts by assessing your performance in real time. Marking is based on the Group Workshop Marking Rubric located in the course site.
On the day of your group workshop, each student needs to complete the Self and Peer Assessment Form which you will find in the Assessment One folder on Blackboard and email it to your Tutor. This process ensures that all students contribute fairly and meaningfully to the group workshop assessment task.
Deferral or extension
You may be able to defer this exam .
Note: Should you be applying for a Deferral for Part B due to illness or an unexpected personal crisis, please indicate on your request that this is an In-Semester Deferred Exam [i.e. not End of Semester Deferred Exam] and specify the week you are referring to i.e. Week 4, Week 5, Week 6 or Week 7.
Late submission
A penalty of 10% of the maximum possible mark will be deducted per 24 hours from time submission is due for up to 7 days. After 7 days, you will receive a mark of 0.
Note: As Part A and Part B must be completed (and Part B submitted) in class time, a late submission penalty does not apply.

assessment_details.task_description: This description is a brief summary of the task. For full details, including the marking rubric, please refer to the course Learn UQ (Blackboard Ultra) site. The aim of the Community Development Project is for students to demonstrate the capacity to design a community project that addresses community need and builds capacity underpinned by community development principles and skills. The project will also meet the course learning objective to demonstrate culturally responsive practice approaches to working with groups and communities. Students will have the opportunity to design a community development project in the form of a funding application. The funding proposal is to be completed on a pre-formatted document. Please adhere to the word counts in each section of your funding application. Project Planning You are expected to engage in a project planning process to develop your community development projects in the tutorials. Tutorial worksheet and activities are designed to support this process. Evidence of project planning is required for this assessment (please refer to the Community Development Project Marking Rubric in the course site ) . Please ensure that you participate in at least one project planning tutorial. These tutorials are in Week 8, Week 9 and Week 10. Your tutor will record your participation as evidence of this requirement. Should you be unable to attend and participate in a project planning tutorial due to ill health or unanticipated personal crisis, then a catch-up worksheet must be completed and submitted to the Tutor to ensure that you have met this course learning outcome. If a student is on a regional placement, then an online project planning tutorial will be organised. Use of AI: This task has been designed to be challenging, authentic and complex. While students may use AI technologies, successful completion of assessment in this course will require students to critically engage in specific contexts and tasks for which artificial intelligence will provide only limited support and guidance. A failure to reference generative AI use may constitute student misconduct under the Student Code of Conduct. To pass this assessment, students will be required to demonstrate detailed comprehension of their written submission independent of AI tools. Read full task description Hide full task description

This assessment requires students to submit an electronic version of their assignment via Blackboard, using the Turnitin software. Please refer to ITS help if you experience difficulties in submitting your assessment in Blackboard or using Turnitin.
Deferral or extension
You may be able to apply for an extension .
The maximum extension allowed is 14 days. Extensions are given in multiples of 24 hours.
Extension requests are submitted online via my.UQ. Extension requests received in any other way will not be approved.
Extension guidelines
Extension requests should be submitted prior to the assessment deadline. Requests for extensions received after the assessment item submission due date may not be approved. Late requests must include evidence of the reasons for the late request as per the guidelines in my.UQ . The extension granted should be in proportion to the period of illness or disruption caused by the exceptional circumstances and will typically be no more than the specified maximum extension length for each assessment. A maximum of three assessment requests can be submitted for each assessment, and the third request must include an Assessment Management Plan. Students who have been ill or unable to attend class for more than 4 weeks in a semester are advised to carefully consider whether they are capable of successfully completing their courses and may need to consider applying for removal of course . Students who have a disability or a chronic medical condition (including a mental health condition) are encouraged to meet with a Disability Advisor within Student Services to request a Student Access Plan (SAP) with a clause on extension requests. Students who have an SAP can apply for a 7-day extension.
Outcome of application
Extension requests are generally processed within 2 working days.
Late submission
A penalty of 10% of the maximum possible mark will be deducted per 24 hours from time submission is due for up to 7 days. After 7 days, you will receive a mark of 0.

learning_activities.topic: Overview and Introduction to the course In this introductory session, we explore group work and community development as methods of social work practice. We examine community as the focus and context of social work practice. Through the course overview, you'll gain an understanding of the course structure, expectations and requirements which will enable you to engage meaningfully with the learning over the next 13 weeks. Please note: There are no tutorials this week. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L04

Community Education Today we focus on the theory and practice of community education. This class will provide the foundation for planning and facilitating your group workshops in Weeks 4-7 of the course. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L04, L05

Introductory Tutorial In this first tutorial, we will introduce ourselves and set group agreements for how we will work together over the semester. We will organise group membership, topics and the schedule for the group workshops and begin to consider community work practice skills. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L04

Culturally Responsive Community Work Today we host a guest practitioner who will guide our learning about protocols for respectful engagement with culturally diverse communities. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L04

Community Education We review community education principles and identify important practice skills for the group workshops. We will undertake reflective activities to prepare for writing workshop reflections. We will discuss approaches to, and skills in, engaging with culturally diverse communities. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L04, L05

Working with Groups in a Community Context We discuss the types of groups in a community work context. We explore the different ways community workers facilitate group participation. This theme will continue in the tutorial. Learning outcomes: L02, L04, L05

Maximising Group Participation This tutorial begins with the first skills workshop which focuses on achieving inclusive group leadership through maximising participation in groups. Students will engage in the first reflective journaling activity. We will discuss material from the course readings with a focus on the stage theory of groups. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L04

Groups as Vehicles for Change We return to the theme of working with groups and consider some practical examples of how community groups are being used to achieve positive social change. Learning outcomes: L02, L04, L05

Managing Conflict in Groups The second student skills workshop addresses the topic of understanding and managing conflict in groups. We discuss conflict as an inevitable part of groups and consider how conflict can be managed constructively. Students will engage in the second reflective journaling activity. Learning outcomes: L02, L04
Asset Based Community Development We explore the principles of an Asset Based Approach to Community Development. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L04

Assessing Community Needs & Capacities Assessing a community's needs and capacities is the topic of today's group workshop. We will discuss the Asset-Based Community Development (ABCD) approach. Students will engage in their third reflective journaling activity. Learning outcomes: L03, L04, L05
A Critical Practice Perspective We consider critical forms of community work that are aimed at creating social change. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L04

Working with the Media The final skills workshop addresses working with the media (print or social media) to represent and advocate for your community. Students learn the skill of preparing media releases in community practice. We consider whether generative AI can play a role. Students will engage in their final reflective journaling activity. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L04

Community Consultation and Advocacy Today we explore the social worker's role in representing and advocating for/with communities through community consultative processes. Learning outcomes: L03, L04, L05

Community Consultation Processes Project Planning: In this tutorial, we commence the process of planning your community development project. A tutorial worksheet and activities are designed to support this process. Note: You are expected to engage in the project planning process. Evidence of project planning is required for Assessment Two (please refer to the Community Development Project Marking Rubric in the course site ) . Your tutor will record your participation as evidence of this requirement. Learning outcomes: L03, L04, L05

Community Work Practice & Policy Processes We continue to explore community consultation processes from a practice perspective. We focus on the social work role and writing an advocacy paper. Learning outcomes: L03, L04, L05

Community Consultation Processes Project Planning: In this tutorial, we continue to explore community consultation processes and work together to discuss and plan your community development project. Note: You are expected to engage in the project planning process. Evidence of project planning is required for Assessment Two (please refer to the Community Development Project Marking Rubric in the course site ) . Your tutor will record your participation as evidence of this requirement. Learning outcomes: L03, L04, L05

Preparing your Funding Proposal Part 1 We consider how social workers in community practice access funds for community activities. We discuss the following elements of your funding submission for your community development project: writing a budget, timeline and milestones. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03, L04, L05

Preparing your Funding Proposal Part 1 In this tutorial, we conclude the project planning phase. We will focus on the skills involved in writing a funding submission. The class will engage in writing exercises. Note: You are expected to engage in the project planning process. Evidence of project planning is required for Assessment Two (please refer to the Community Development Project Marking Rubric in the course site ) . Your tutor will record your participation as evidence of this requirement. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03, L04, L05

Preparing your Funding Proposal Part 2 We continue to focus on the funding submission for your community development project and consider all the components. We discuss the community development principles and values underpinning your project design. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03, L04, L05

Preparing your Funding Proposal Part 2 In this tutorial we continue to focus on the practice skills involved in writing a funding submission. We will engage in activities that will support you to reflect on the community development principles and skills that underpin your project design. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03, L04, L05
Implementation, Evaluation and Review Part 1 Today we focus on project evaluation processes to support this important element of the funding submission. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03, L04, L05
Implementation, Evaluation and Review Part 1 In this tutorial we engage in learning activities to explore and discuss project evaluation processes. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03, L04, L05

Implementation, Evaluation and Review Part 2 In the final lecture, we conclude our discussions of the funding submission and evaluation processes. Key course themes will be reviewed. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03, L04, L05

Course Review In the first half of the tutorial we review your learning in the course. In the last half we celebrate your achievements over the semester - activities to be decided together! Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03, L04, L05
